 Palace hits back at VP Sara camp over admin coercion claim
 by 
 Ruth Abbey Carlos
 Nov 17, 2026
 1:22 PM GMT+8
 Palace Press Officer Claire Castro (PNA file photo by Ruth Abbey Gita-Carlos) 
 MANILA – Malacañang on Tuesday defended President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. against allegations by Vice President Sara Duterte’s camp that the administration is using government agencies to coerce individuals into becoming witnesses against her.
 In a statement, Palace Press Officer Claire Castro said Marcos remains focused on national development and strengthening the country’s relations with members of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) and its dialogue partners.
 Castro said the President’s priorities include economic recovery, addressing energy concerns, and advancing initiatives in technology, agriculture and education.
 “Hindi po gawain sa panahon ngayon ang gumawa ng intriga at magplanta ng ebidensya kung saan sanay at hasa ang [mga] Duterte (Creating intrigue and planting evidence are not practices of the present administration, unlike the Duterte camp, which is well-versed and experienced in such tactics),” she said.
 Castro issued the statement after Duterte’s spokesperson, lawyer Salvador Paolo Panelo Jr., raised alarm over an alleged threat and coercion against a former household staff member of the Vice President in Manila.
 Panelo said the former staff member sought Duterte’s help through a text message at around 11:19 p.m. on Monday.
 Panelo added the former staff member claimed to be under the custody or control of “certain individuals.”
 The staff member was allegedly being “forced to sign a document” but had refused to do so.
 Duterte’s camp expressed concern that the incident could be part of what it described as the government’s “unremitting efforts” to harass, threaten and coerce individuals into becoming false witnesses.
 It also accused the Marcos administration of using institutions such as the National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) to carry out its “relentless campaign” against the Vice President.
 The camp likewise called for immediate measures to ensure the former staff member’s safety and establish the person's whereabouts.
 Castro said the allegations raised by the Vice President’s camp should be investigated.
 “Ang pag iimbestiga sa nasabing kwento kung may katotohanan ay nararapat lamang (Investigating the said allegations to determine whether they are true is only appropriate),” she said. 
 Meanwhile, Senator Panfilo Lacson said an “honest mistake” can be a double-edged sword, in reaction to former chief presidential legal counsel Salvador Panelo's claim that Duterte committed an honest mistake when she included GenCorp Industries, Inc. in her Statement of Assets, Liabilities and Net Worth (SALN).
 "'HONEST MISTAKE': It is a double-edged sword. Its meaning depends on the state of mind and intent of the person behind it. It can be an inadvertent slip that exposes the truth, or a genuine blind spot that mistakes falsehood for reality," Lacson said in a post on X on Tuesday.
 "Ultimately, only the person responsible can say which is which," he added.
 In a television interview earlier this week, Panelo said despite her mistake, Duterte acted in good faith when she listed GenCorp as a business interest.
 Duterte is facing an impeachment trial before the Senate over allegations of betrayal of public trust, culpable violation of the Constitution and other offenses, including alleged misuse of confidential funds, unexplained wealth, and threats against Marcos, his wife, and former House Speaker Martin Romualdez.
 GenCorp figured in the proceedings under Article II of the Articles of Impeachment, which covers allegations involving Duterte's wealth declarations and alleged failure to divest from business interests upon assuming public office.
 The prosecution presented Duterte's 2024 and 2025 SALNs, which listed GenCorp among her business interests. It also cited the company's government contracts with the Davao City government, led by her brother, Mayor Sebastian Duterte, as part of its examination of possible conflicts of interest. (With a report from Leonel Abasola/PNA)
